This article is devoted to the development of methodological approaches to wetsuit design based on the classification of water sports. The goal of this research is to create innovative wetsuits adapted to the specifics of water sports, increasing reliability and protective properties, while improving comfort and performance. The subject of the study is the "person-wetsuit-aquatic environment" system, with a particular focus on protecting the wearer from external factors by developing rational variants of wetsuit components, taking into account ergonomics and the dynamic conformity of the product. The article proposes a systematic classification of aquatic sports, taking into account the nature of the aquatic environment, the degree of its control, temperature parameters, and the requirements for protective equipment. A model for the combination of the type of sports discipline and the characteristics of wetsuits (neoprene thickness, design, and mandatory application conditions) has been developed. Special attention was paid to the water sport "slalom" as a sport with maximum hydrodynamic variability and increased thermal protection requirements. The dependence of equipment selection on temperature ranges, flow velocity, and wind conditions has been substantiated. The presented classification can be used in the development of new types of wetsuits with enhanced protective properties, as well as in athlete training, regulatory requirements, and improvement of training logistics.

Traditional scientometric analysis methods primarily rely on binary keyword associations, which limits the ability to capture complex research structures. This study proposes a multi-association rule-based method (MAR) that enables the extraction of higher-order (n-ary) associations among keywords to address the stated limitation. The method integrates the Apriori algorithm with knowledge graph visualization to quantitatively analyse multi-keyword associations. The proposed method is applied to the Building Information Modelling (BIM) research domain. The bibliometric data, comprising 12,185 publications, is retrieved from the Scopus database following a systematic refinement of the initial search results to the architecture, engineering, construction, and operation (AECO)-relevant literature. The results demonstrate that the MAR method effectively identifies complex research patterns. The framework advances traditional scientometric tools by enabling the identification of multi-keyword semantic associations with quantified strength metrics (support, confidence, lift). Emerging trends revealed by the regression analysis include the convergence of BIM with generative artificial intelligence, real-time data integration, explainable AI, and human-centric approaches. The findings provide a scalable and analytical approach for identifying interdisciplinary research trends and gaps. The proposed method enables a deeper understanding of complex knowledge structures while supporting strategic decision-making and technology adoption.

Future fighter operations are expected to combine increasingly capable autonomy, collaborative aircraft, dense sensor information, and sustained physiological and cognitive demands. This Perspective proposes a pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework in which the pilot, a pilot-specific digital twin, an intelligent flight-management system, the aircraft, and external agents are treated as interdependent elements within a systems-of-systems framework. The framework does not replace situation awareness, distributed cognition, joint cognitive systems, adaptive automation, or human-autonomy teaming. Instead, it extends their unit of analysis by making the pilot’s dynamic physiological and neurocognitive state, longitudinal variability, and health-related constraints explicit system variables and design objectives. The pilot digital twin is defined narrowly as an individualized state-estimation and forecasting capability, whereas the intelligent flight-management system integrates pilot, platform, mission, and environmental information to provide explainable recommendations and, where authorized, bounded adaptive action. We identify testable propositions concerning individualized prediction, adaptive support, shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and governance. The framework is prospective and requires validation in simulation, training, and operationally representative environments. Its purpose is to organize research toward systems that protect pilot agency, sustain performance, and preserve long-term health while exploiting increasingly autonomous teammates.

Electronic learning (e-learning) or online learning in medical education has become increasingly prevalent, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, poor student engagement and reduced motivation are among the critical challenges associated with online learning. The e-learning for Renal Applied Pharmacology (e-RAP) is a new technology-enhanced learning tool that includes a nephron image augmented with several Quick Response (QR) codes. It allows students to access relevant QR-linked educational materials prepared by the teachers. This quasi-experimental pilot study examined whether use of the e-RAP tool was associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation among 105 preclinical medical students at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA), Malaysia. Participants in the intervention group (Year 2, n = 45) used the e-RAP tool, while the control group (Year 1, n = 60) received conventional teaching. Cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation scores were measured using pre- and posttest multiple-choice questions (MCQ), the Burch Engagement Survey for Students, and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, respectively. Both groups demonstrated improvements in mean cognitive scores from pre- to post-test MCQ, with greater gains in the intervention group than in the control group. The intervention group was also associated with higher emotional and cognitive engagement (both in and out of class) and higher scores in several motivational domains, including intrinsic value, cognitive strategy use, and selfregulation. Although groups differed by academic year, baseline knowledge was comparable. Taken together, these preliminary findings suggest that e-RAP use may be associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation.

Abstract Despite the increasing adoption of automated/autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs) in precision agriculture, existing human-machine interfaces (HMIs) remain function-centric, frequently neglecting the cognitive and user experience (UX) needs of non-technical operators. Consequently, current dashboards suffer from limited usability, high cognitive load, and reduced system transparency, increasing the risk of operator error. To address this gap within agricultural teleoperation interface design, this study presents a theory-driven HMI framework that systematically translates Endsley’s Situational Awareness (SA) theory (Perception, Comprehension, Projection) and ISO 9241 ergonomic principles into a structured three-panel AGV teleoperation interface. Unlike conventional function-oriented dashboards, the proposed framework organises interface components according to operator cognitive requirements to support information perception, comprehension, and projection during remote operation. A theory-driven agricultural teleoperation HMI framework was developed by translating cognitive and ergonomic principles into practical interface organization strategies. To formatively evaluate this SA-driven design architecture, we conducted a user-perception study with non-expert digitally literate participants (N = 20), evaluating three iterative HMI prototypes. The comparative results indicate that the SA-aligned layout received higher user ratings in perceived decision-support capability (SA3), cognitive workload reduction, and overall usability compared with baseline designs during formative evaluation. The study provides preliminary methodological guidance for agricultural teleoperation HMI design, while recognizing that objective operational validation with target agricultural users remains necessary.

Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) writing instruction, yet the mechanisms through which AI integration may improve written English proficiency (WEP) remain theoretically fragmented. Objective: This systematic review synthesises literature published within the 2018–2026 review window, together with foundational theoretical works, to develop a structural-equation-modelling (SEM) framework in which self-regulated learning (SRL), learner engagement, self-efficacy, and AI literacy operate as parallel and serial mediators between AI integration and WEP. Method: Following a structured thematic-synthesis approach, the reviewed literature was organised around four connected domains: AI-supported writing instruction, generative-AI adoption, learner and teacher perceptions, and self-regulated learning in AI-supported contexts. The synthesis then examined evidence for direct, mediating, and serial relationships among the focal constructs. Key findings: The literature provides partial support for the individual links connecting AI integration, the proposed mediators, and language-learning outcomes; however, these pathways are rarely tested within a single integrated model. Evidence for mediation remains fragmented, the proposed serial chain is largely untested, and Jordanian and broader Levantine contexts remain under-represented relative to East Asian and Gulf settings. Implications: The review proposes fourteen hypotheses: nine direct-effect hypotheses (H1–H9) and five mediation hypotheses (H10a–H10e), including one serial mediation chain, as a framework for future quantitative validation among English majors at public Jordanian universities.

documents.abstract: Abstract The World Wide Web has evolved from a predominantly static information environment into an increasingly interactive, semantic, distributed and intelligent digital ecosystem. The earlier study on Web 1.0 to Web 3.0 described the transition from the read-only web to the read-write social web and then toward the semantic web. This revised study extends that framework to Web 4.0 and examines the technological and conceptual changes across the four stages. Web 1.0 is characterized by static pages, one-way information delivery and limited user participation; Web 2.0 emphasizes interaction, user-generated content, social networking and web applications; Web 3.0 is associated with semantic interoperability, decentralized architectures, data ownership and intelligent processing; and Web 4.0 is increasingly discussed as an intelligent or symbiotic web in which artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), cloud/edge computing, augmented and virtual reality, machine-to-machine communication and autonomous agents can interact with people and each other. The literature does not provide one universally accepted definition of Web 4.0, so this paper treats it as an emerging research and technology paradigm rather than a fixed technical standard. The study also discusses implications for libraries and information services, including intelligent discovery, personalized services, virtual assistance, semantic knowledge organization and human-machine collaboration. The paper concludes that the movement from Web 1.0 to Web 4.0 represents a shift from information access toward participation, meaning, intelligence and increasingly symbiotic interaction.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare systems is rapidly increasing in India, with the market estimated to grow from $0.83 billion in 2023 to $17.75 billion by 2032. Employee satisfaction remains a major concern that relevant studies in the healthcare sector have yet to address. This article explores how AI integration is affecting employee satisfaction in India’s healthcare industry. The healthcare industry faces a 60% shortage of digital skills; 47% of Indian healthcare workers are not digitally literate, and only 34% of organizations are advancing toward piloting AI projects, despite 86% having adopted AI. Implementation challenges include limited technical expertise among clinicians, the psychological burden of increased monitoring, poor rural infrastructure, data privacy concerns, and workforce constraints. For AI to succeed, it must be presented as a supplement to workers, not a replacement. This shift should include targeted training to address digital literacy gaps, governance that incorporates clinician input in system design, and ongoing staffing support. Existing evidence suggests that AI adoption may be associated with burnout and reduced employee satisfaction when it is not coupled with these integrated efforts. Beyond technical expertise, research highlights human-centered design, thorough training for healthcare professionals, and maintaining autonomy as key drivers of effective AI integration in healthcare in India. To benefit from AI, healthcare facilities in India must adopt modern technology. They must also prioritize staff well-being.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of China’s low fertility rate, examining the impact of pet ownership on fertility intentions and its underlying mechanisms holds significant importance for enriching research on factors influencing fertility decisions and for understanding the complex relationship between modern lifestyles and reproductive choices. This study, grounded in self-determination theory, collected 551 valid samples through questionnaire surveys and employed structural equation modeling for analysis. Findings reveal that pet ownership not only positively associated with fertility intentions but also indirectly affects them through mediating variables such as fertility motivation, intrinsic needs, and emotional value. Pet ownership appears to individuals’ positive expectations toward parenthood by providing opportunities for daily care, emotional companionship, and responsibility-taking; simultaneously, the nurturing experience and emotional bonds cultivated through pet ownership activate individuals’ intrinsic motivation toward the role of “parenthood.” This may fulfill fundamental psychological needs such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness, thereby strengthening reproductive motivation. The positive emotional experiences and heightened confidence in family life derived from pet ownership may significantly reduce sensitivity to reproductive pressures, indirectly supporting the willingness to have children. This study provides theoretical support and empirical evidence for understanding the relationship between pet ownership and fertility intentions, as well as for formulating relevant policies.

Introduction To explore the psychological mechanisms of persistence in adult instrumental learning, this study investigates the associations among different types of teacher feedback, self-efficacy, and intrinsic motivation, and examines the moderating role of learning stages. Methods Using a cross-sectional survey design, scale and open-ended text data were collected from 743 adult violin learners. A moderated mediation model was tested through multiple regression and the Bootstrap method, supplemented by thematic analysis to provide a qualitative context. Results Data analysis indicates: (1) Positive feedback and constructive feedback are significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001; β = 0.342, p < 0.001), while negative feedback shows a significant negative association ( β = −0.318, p < 0.001); (2) Self-efficacy demonstrates a significant partial mediating association between the three types of feedback and intrinsic motivation, with indirect effect estimates of 0.103, 0.098, and −0.097, respectively (95% CIs all exclude 0); (3) The learning stage significantly moderates the conditional indirect effects: as the learning stage advances, the indirect association of positive feedback on intrinsic motivation via self-efficacy gradually weakens (index of moderated mediation = −0.045), whereas the indirect association of constructive feedback gradually strengthens (index of moderated mediation = 0.038). Open-ended texts echo these statistical paths at the micro-level. Discussion The study shows that there are heterogeneous and dynamic statistical connections between teacher feedback and adult intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy is a key pathway to understanding this connection. In practice, the provision of instructional feedback content should match the learners’ experience stage.

Abstract The increasing deployment of AI agents in operations management, spanning production scheduling, predictive maintenance, supply chain management, and energy systems, is progressively shifting automated systems from decision support tools to autonomous decision-making entities. Despite this transition, existing frameworks do not adequately characterize how humans and AI agents interact in operational decision-making contexts. This paper proposes a taxonomy of human-AI interaction patterns in agent-based operations management, developed through a theory-driven approach based on decision theory, control systems, human factors, and explainable AI research. The taxonomy articulates the interaction space along five analytically separable dimensions: Decision Trigger, Execution Authority, Human Entry Point, Human Influence and Interpretive Access. It identifies seven interaction patterns organized into four macro-patterns ordered by increasing AI operational autonomy. Illustrative examples drawn from scientific literature demonstrate the discriminative capacity of the taxonomy across heterogeneous operations management domains and agent architectures. The taxonomy provides researchers with an analytical instrument to characterize and compare human-AI decision loop configurations, and practitioners with a design reference for deliberate and accountable interaction choices in operational AI deployments.

Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) integration in online presentation assessment has expanded rapidly; however, existing facial emotion recognition systems in education remain largely focused on surveillance and behavioral monitoring, with limited validation against human judgment and insufficient attention to ethical and character-development dimensions. Purpose. This study aimed to develop and validate a virtual reality (VR)-based multimodal assessment framework for evaluating presentation integrity among higher education students. Method. A design science research approach was employed involving 64 students from two parallel classes (A1, n = 33; A2, n = 31) at a university in South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Data from expert validation, technical performance evaluation, NASA-TLX, System Usability Scale, and lecturer assessments were analyzed using content validity analysis with modified kappa, classification metrics, Bland-Altman agreement analysis, and descriptive statistics. Novelty. This study introduces a human-centered AI-VR assessment approach that integrates facial emotion recognition, gaze detection, and cognitive load measurement into a reflective Presentation Integrity Index. Unlike conventional AI-based monitoring systems that generate binary judgments, the proposed framework emphasizes ethical interpretation by combining affective, behavioral, and cognitive indicators to support formative character-based assessment. Results. The framework demonstrated satisfactory content validity (S-CVI/Ave = 0.83), although refinement of several indicators was required. Emotion and gaze modules achieved accuracy levels of 85.3% and 89.0%, respectively. The Presentation Integrity Index showed 93.8% agreement with lecturer assessments, moderate cognitive load (NASA-TLX = 46.7), and good usability (SUS = 76.4). Conclusion. The proposed AI-VR framework provides an ethical and reflective approach for character-based presentation assessment while requiring broader validation involving multiple evaluators and diverse educational contexts.

Mooring operations are among the most hazardous activities in maritime transportation and continue to cause injuries and fatalities. Although accident investigation reports provide information on contributing factors, their use in human reliability assessment (HRA) remains limited. This study proposes an accident-informed framework to estimate human error probability (HEP) in ship mooring operations by integrating the Success Likelihood Index Method (SLIM) with the Entropy Weight Method (EWM). Thirty-five accident investigation reports were analysed to identify performance shaping factors (PSFs) associated with human error. The PSFs were transformed into an occurrence matrix, weighted using entropy analysis, and incorporated into SLIM to estimate HEP values for tasks. The execution-related mechanism (T6.1) yielded a slightly higher accident-informed HEP than the perception-related mechanism (T6.3) (6.42 × 10 −4 vs. 5.67 × 10 −4 ) and a higher frequency-based risk contribution index (0.0122 vs. 0.00738). Within Task T6, two main failure mechanisms were identified: execution-related failures associated with line handling and perception-related failures associated with hazard recognition. T6.1 represented the higher-priority mechanism within the analysed accident sample because it combined a slightly higher HEP with higher accident occurrence frequency. The findings support practical priorities for mooring safety, including coordinated command and execution, safe crew positioning, proper line handling, continuous situational awareness, and scenario-based onboard drills.

Mobile GUI Agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise in human-computer intelligence. However, current research primarily focuses on reactive task execution while lacking a comprehensive “understanding-prediction-execution” process for user intentions, which are the core requirements of active agents. In this paper, we propose the Act2Intention framework that builds an active mobile agent by integrating understanding, predicting user intentions, and executing decisions. Firstly, we constructed the Act2Intention Bench through collection and validated generation, comprising 72,511 intentions and over 700,000 actions across 52 apps, thereby establishing the first benchmark for evaluating proactive agents via continuous “intention-actions” trajectories. We further develop the Act2Intention Agent, achieving proactive services through Proactive-oriented Intention Understanding, Personalized Proactive Intention Prediction, and Experience-guided Intention Execution. Experimental results show that supervised fine-tuning on Act2Intention Bench yields absolute improvements of +32.0 Acc-S, +10.25 Acc-S, and +6.9 SSR points over non-fine-tuned counterparts under the same agent framework for intention understanding, prediction, and execution, respectively. This success underscores the necessity and value of the Act2Intention Bench, which establishes a standardized platform for developing and evaluating proactive agents and consequently paves the way for research on intention-driven human-computer interaction. To facilitate further research, we open-source our code and Act2Intention Bench at: npuNancy/Act2Intention.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is widely studied at the organizational level, yet much less is known about the specific algorithms organizations adopt and the reasons for these choices. This study investigates AI adoption among research-and-development (R&D) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups in Turkiye through a proposed expert-driven, learning-domain-based taxonomy comprising 28 algorithms grouped into seven AI families. Survey data were collected from 36 organizations affiliated with the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce. Reliability and validity were established, and adoption was examined through descriptive statistics and non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests. At the algorithm level, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, Multilayer Perceptron, and Linear Regression were the most adopted, reflecting a preference for interpretable, structurally familiar methods, whereas Deep Q-Network, Policy Gradient, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping were the least adopted. At the family level, Unsupervised Learning and Natural Language Processing ranked highest, while Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Behavior recorded the lowest and most divergent adoption. Adoption also varied by sector—Financial/FinTech and Engineering/Defense showed the broadest portfolios and Healthcare and Commerce/e-Commerce the narrowest—with statistically significant cross-sector differences for Autonomous Behavior and Unsupervised Learning. Adoption range increased across organizational stages, peaking at post-incubation. The findings extend the Technology-Organization-Environment framework with diffusion of innovation and dynamic capability theory to the algorithm level and emphasize AI algorithms’ knowledge as a target for SMEs’ digital transformation.

documents.abstract: The swift evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is dramatically changing the landscape of education, especially when it comes to assessment. Traditional methods, which focus heavily on standardized tests and final evaluations, are falling short in capturing the complex cognitive, social, and digital skills that are essential in today’s world. This paper delves into the transformative power of AI in educational assessment and suggests a strategic framework for embracing digital change. By reviewing current literature, the study highlights AI-driven innovations like adaptive testing, automated grading, learning analytics, and competency-based assessment models. It also tackles important challenges such as ethical issues, algorithmic bias, data privacy, and maintaining academic integrity. The paper emphasizes that a comprehensive, policy-oriented, and pedagogically sound approach are crucial for effectively integrating AI into assessment systems. In the end, it offers practical strategies for institutions aiming to update their assessment practices in an AI-enhanced educational environment.

Abstract Viksit Bharat 2047 will not be achieved through infrastructure and technology alone. Much of the change will be visible in ordinary routines: the way electricity and water are used at home, the way waste is handled, the products people choose, and the willingness of communities to take part in local environmental efforts. Advertising is relevant here because it already knows how to reach large audiences, tell memorable stories and influence everyday choices. Advertising itself is changing quickly. Artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), spatial computing and algorithmic personalisation are giving audiences more interactive forms of communication. This paper considers what these developments could mean for sustainability campaigns. The main concern is a familiar one: people may genuinely care about environmental issues and still struggle to turn that concern into consistent behaviour. The discussion draws on secondary material relating to the IndiaAI Mission, NITI Aayog policy directions, Sustainable Development Goal 12 and media-effects research. On this basis, the paper develops the AI-Immersive Sustainable Advertising Behaviour Model (AISABM). It brings together five connected ideas: context-sensitive communication, immersive experience, trustworthy information, a simple route to action, and feedback based on observable behaviour. Technology can also create a new divide if access is taken for granted. High-end VR is unlikely to be equally available to everyone, whereas radio, podcasts, smartphones and lightweight AR applications can travel much further. This is why the paper does not present immersive media as a replacement for older channels. It argues for a combination of both. The discussion also considers surveillance, manipulation, greenwashing and the energy cost of AI itself. The larger argument is that sustainability advertising has to do more than ask people to 'be green'. A useful campaign should make the issue understandable, connect it with everyday life, provide evidence people can trust and make the next step reasonably easy. Where possible, that step should also be observable over time.

ABSTRACT Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have progressed rapidly over the past decade. As the core functional layer, the intrinsic properties of perovskite materials, including band structure, carrier transport, and optical response, strongly influence PSC performance. Theoretical calculations support absorber screening and device‐performance prediction. However, most studies remain confined to either materials‐level investigation or device‐level evaluation, without a general framework linking microscopic material properties to macroscopic device performance. To address this gap, we develop a large language model (LLM)‐driven, materials‐to‐device cross‐scale agentic framework that establishes a closed‐loop workflow from first‐principles descriptor extraction to solar‐cell performance optimization. A Manager Agent coordinates density functional theory (DFT)‐based materials calculations, drift‐diffusion device simulation, and Bayesian optimization of PSC architectures. Through the model context protocol (MCP), 55 in‐house tools and analysis/simulation programs are encapsulated and orchestrated as callable skills, enabling human‐in‐the‐loop review, cross‐scale parameter transfer, task‐state control, simulation execution, provenance tracking, and error recovery. Across 24 multi‐turn sessions and 60 benchmark turns, the agent achieved a pass rate of 96.7%, significantly outperforming OpenClaw (60.0%). This work provides an extensible methodological route for traceable, auditable, and closed‐loop cross‐scale research on PSCs.

Primary education represents the foundational stage of formal education, where children develop essential academic, cognitive, social, emotional, creative, and communication skills. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into primary education offers new possibilities for personalized learning, interactive instruction, educational games, language development, accessibility, formative assessment, and teacher support. However, the use of AI at the primary level requires particular care because young learners may have limited ability to understand technological risks, evaluate AI-generated information, or protect their personal information independently. Therefore, AI should be introduced in an age-appropriate, safe, inclusive, and teacher-guided manner. The fundamental principle of AI in primary education is: Child → Teacher Guidance → AI-Supported Learning → Interaction → Feedback → Learning AI should support the educational process rather than replace teachers, parents, classroom interaction, play, creativity, or children's independent thinking.Artificial Intelligence in primary education refers to the use of AI-enabled technologies to support teaching, learning, assessment, educational communication, and the overall development of young learners. AI applications can provide personalized learning activities, interactive exercises, intelligent tutoring, language support, educational games, automated feedback, and assistive learning facilities. Examples of AI applications in primary education include intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, educational chatbots, speech-recognition applications, AI-supported language-learning systems, educational games, automated feedback tools, and AI-assisted teaching resources. The main purpose of AI at this level is to enhance the learning experience while keeping the teacher and the learner at the centre of education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity, volatility, and sustainability pressures affecting global supply chains have accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in logistics management. Among these AI approaches, Intelligent Agents (IAs) and Multi-agent Systems (MAS) have emerged as essential tools for supporting decentralized, adaptive, event-driven, and real-time decision-making processes in dynamic logistics environments. Unlike traditional centralized planning systems, agent-based approaches enable autonomous entities such as suppliers, warehouses, transportation units, and distribution centers to coordinate actions, exchange information, and manage variability. This paper presents a structured literature review of peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science on the use of AI agents to support decision-making in logistics management and supply chain operations. Particular attention is given to the strategic importance of intelligent agents in strengthening resilience, operational efficiency, and sustainability in increasingly uncertain logistics systems. The findings indicate that intelligent agents improve decision quality, responsiveness, coordination, and resource utilization across distributed logistics networks. Furthermore, Multi-Agent Systems enhance interoperability and collaboration among logistics actors, enabling more agile and resilient supply chains. However, challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, governance, scalability, and human–AI collaboration continue to limit large-scale implementation in industrial environments.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Digital Economy are increasingly shaping India's economic transformation. Their applications in agriculture, manufacturing, services, banking, education, healthcare, governance and entrepreneurship have the potential to improve productivity, reduce transaction costs, expand access to services and strengthen innovation. This study examines the economic role of AI and digitalisation with particular reference to sustainable development and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. The study is based on secondary data and follows a descriptive and analytical approach. Official statistics on internet connectivity, digital payments and the IndiaAI Mission are used to provide a quantitative dimension to the analysis. The evidence shows rapid expansion of India's digital ecosystem: internet subscribers reached 1,028.61 million by December 2025, while rural internet subscribers stood at 407.69 million in March 2025. UPI processed 22,716.07 million transactions worth ₹28,92,138.67 crore in June 2026. The IndiaAI Mission, approved with an outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore, has expanded compute capacity beyond its initial 10,000-GPU target. The study concludes that AI and digitalisation can support productivity, financial inclusion, entrepreneurship, sustainable resource use and public-service delivery. However, digital inequality, skill gaps, data privacy, cybersecurity, employment restructuring and environmental costs require policy attention. Inclusive infrastructure, human-capital development, responsible AI and sustainable digital practices are therefore essential for Viksit Bharat 2047.

documents.abstract: Abstract India's journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047 requires a transformation that combines technological advancement with inclusive and sustainable economic development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) have emerged as two important pillars of this transformation. While DPI provides the digital foundations for identity, payments, data exchange, and access to public and private services, AI can add intelligence, automation, personalization, and predictive capabilities to these systems. Together, they can significantly improve governance, healthcare, education, agriculture, financial inclusion, digital commerce, and public service delivery. This paper examines the role of AI-enabled Digital Public Infrastructure in building a developed India by 2047. It explores opportunities, challenges, ethical considerations, and the need for responsible and inclusive AI adoption. The paper argues that India's competitive advantage will depend not merely on technological adoption but on developing trusted, accessible, secure, multilingual, and citizen-centric digital ecosystems. Strengthening digital skills, cybersecurity, data governance, research and innovation, and public-private partnerships will be essential for realizing this vision. AI combined with DPI can become a powerful foundation for inclusive prosperity, innovation, and sustainable development in Viksit Bharat.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is getting integrated into the day-to-day life of every human being. This fast-changing technology is transforming traditional technology, society and governance at a rapid pace. This paper explores the emerging Technorapid Age, where technological change may move faster than the ability of individuals, institutions and governance systems to adapt. It focuses on Responsible Innovation as a methodology to manage this growing gap. It proposes that AI development should not be measured only by technological progress. It should also consider human well-being, social inclusion, ethical responsibility and effective governance. It examines the relationship between AI, technology and society. It highlights the need for human adaptability, accountability and responsible decision-making. The author proposes that Responsible Innovation can help create an equilibrium between technological acceleration and human adaptive capacity. The paper directly connects with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. India needs technological development that is innovative, inclusive, ethical and sustainable. Technology should support human dignity, social well-being and the needs of future generations. The research concludes that achieving Viksit Bharat 2047 requires comprehensive and responsible AI technologies. These innovations should benefit all sections of society (सर्वजन हिताय, सर्वजन सुखाय) and ensure that people are skilled and supported to handle challenges of the Technorapid Age.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of India's digital transformation. It is expected to impact governance, education, healthcare, finance, employment and everyday life as India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. However, this rapid development and adoption of technology also creates a growing gap between technological progress and the ability of individuals and society to adapt. This paper describes this condition as Technorapid, an accelerating pace of technological change that can exceed human, social, institutional and ethical adaptive capacity. The paper proposes that digital transformation should not remain confined to policies and institutional documents. Its success should ultimately be visible on the ground, in the lived experience of its citizens. AI-driven development needs to be evaluated through its ability to improve access, dignity, inclusion, education, employment and quality of life. This paper explores Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the principle that the world is one family, as a philosophical foundation for a human-centered approach to AI ethics. It argues that India's technological progress should be complemented by human adaptation, ethical governance and mechanisms that ensure that the benefits of AI reach diverse sections of society. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of India's digital transformation. It is expected to impact governance, education, healthcare, finance, employment and everyday life as India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. However, this rapid development and adoption of technology also creates a growing gap between technological progress and the ability of individuals and society to adapt. This paper describes this condition as Technorapid, an accelerating pace of technological change that can exceed human, social, institutional and ethical adaptive capacity. The paper proposes that digital transformation should not remain confined to policies and institutional documents. Its success should ultimately be visible on the ground, in the lived experience of its citizens. AI-driven development needs to be evaluated through its ability to improve access, dignity, inclusion, education, employment and quality of life. This paper explores Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the principle that the world is one family, as a philosophical foundation for a human-centered approach to AI ethics. It argues that India's technological progress should be complemented by human adaptation, ethical governance and mechanisms that ensure that the benefits of AI reach diverse sections of society. The paper concludes that the true measure of Viksit Bharat @2047 should not be how advanced India's technologies become, but how meaningfully those technologies improve human live and national progress

Abstract: The present research paper deals with AI generated literature and changing concepts of authorship in the period where AI has replaced every sphere of human life. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has altered assumptions about literary text as the production of human creativity because AI is able to produce poems, stories, essays and other literary forms in response to the simple prompts. As a result, the conventional distinctions between author and reader have become more complicated now. However, the developments questioning the role of authorship into literary studies are not new; rather 20th century literary theory has already challenged the idea of the author as the sole creator of textual meaning. Roland Barthes’ The Death of Author, Michel Foucault’s What Is an Author, T. S. Eliot’s theory of impersonality and W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley’s critique pertaining to intentional fallacy displaced the image of the author and demonstrated that literary meaning is produced through language and discourse without considering the intentions of an author. Generative AI further intensifies these theoretical questions by introducing non-human agents into the process of textual production. Thus, the present paper attempts to put forth the role of AI in production of literary text within the frameworks of theories mentioned above.

The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI) tools, in higher education has created significant opportunities in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting processes, while also raising important questions regarding academic integrity, accuracy, ethical responsibility, and human oversight. To promote informed and responsible use of AI while benefiting from the opportunities it offers, this study presents a framework for the ethical, critical, and responsible use of AI in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting in higher education. AI literacy is conceptualized not merely as the ability to use AI tools, but as the competence to evaluate and verify AI-generated information, establish ethical boundaries, and maintain academic responsibility. The study is designed as a narrative literature review and thematic evaluation based on academic studies and policy and guidance documents published by international organizations. The literature is examined in the contexts of AI literacy, generative AI, research ethics, academic integrity, thesis writing, source verification, and academic reporting. The findings indicate that AI can be used as a supportive tool in academic processes; however, scientific evaluation, source verification, methodological decision-making, and ultimate academic responsibility should remain with humans. The study argues that responsible AI use in higher education should be grounded in the principles of human oversight, critical thinking, verification, transparency, data privacy, and academic integrity. Accordingly, AI literacy should be regarded not merely as a technological skill but as a fundamental component of future academic and research competencies in higher education. The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities for personalized learning, although its contribution to student achievement remains theoretically and empirically contested. Purpose. This study examined the direct and indirect effects of AI use on conceptual understanding and problem-solving ability through learning motivation, locus of control, and learning preferences. Method. A quantitative explanatory design was employed with 88 pre-service teachers enrolled in an Instructional Media course at a teacher education institution in Central Java, Indonesia. Data were collected using validated questionnaires and cognitive assessments. Preliminary analyses were conducted using SPSS, while the measurement and structural models were evaluated through PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. Novelty. This study simultaneously tested three psychological and learning-related mediators within a single structural model, thereby extending previous research that primarily examined the direct relationship between AI use and academic performance. Results. AI use significantly predicted learning motivation and locus of control but did not significantly influence learning preferences. Learning motivation significantly predicted learning outcomes and mediated the relationship between AI use and learning outcomes. In contrast, locus of control and learning preferences showed no significant mediating effects. The direct effect of AI use on learning outcomes was also nonsignificant. Conclusion. AI contributes to student learning primarily by strengthening learning motivation rather than through direct technological exposure. Effective AI integration should therefore emphasize reflective, autonomous, and cognitively engaging learning activities.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into teleconsultation, but its effects on clinician performance remain uncertain. We assessed whether clinician-facing AI improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces referrals or testing, and increases clinician confidence compared with standard teleconsultation or conventional resources. Methods: This retrospectively registered systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 and Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE, publisher-indexed platforms, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, and backward and forward citation searches were performed from inception to 1 August 2026. Eligible studies evaluated clinician-facing AI in adult primary, urgent, or general medical teleconsultation or in high-fidelity virtual consultation designs and reported diagnostic, referral/testing, or confidence outcomes. One reviewer screened records, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using the design-appropriate QUADAS-2, RoB 2, and ROBINS-I domains, with a second pass for consistency. Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the results were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 31 records identified, 25 remained after duplicate removal, 18 full texts were assessed, and six studies were included: two randomized virtual experiments, two retrospectives virtual care cohorts, one randomized crossover conversational AI study, and one provider-to-provider telemedicine case series. In a telehealth screening experiment, AI improved diagnostic prediction, but physicians given a large language model showed no significant benefit (adjusted difference, two percentage points; 95% CI, −4 to 8). Across 102,059 virtual encounters, an AI-generated differential included the clinician’s final diagnosis in 84.2%, although the reference was not independent. AI-assisted urgent care recommendations were rated optimal more often than final physician recommendations (77.1% vs. 67.1%). AI did not reduce unnecessary referrals; one experiment found more confirmatory testing requests and lower trust than with a familiar clinical score. Certainty was low or very low for the principal clinical outcomes. Conclusions: AI may support teleconsultation decisions, but evidence that it reduces unnecessary referrals or meaningfully increases clinician confidence is insufficient. Pragmatic trials using independent patient-level reference standards are needed. Registration: This completed review was retrospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF); no protocol was published before study selection.

documents.abstract: Abstract The eri silkworm, Samia ricini (Lepidoptera: Saturniidae), is an economically important polyphagous silk-producing insect whose productivity is influenced by host-plant quality, digestive physiology, larval development and associated gut microorganisms. The midgut represents a major interface between dietary nutrients and physiological utilization, while the resident microbial community may contribute to nutrient transformation and host adaptation. Although previous studies have independently investigated digestive enzymes, host-plant effects and gut microbial diversity in S. ricini, an integrated predictive framework combining biochemical, microbiome and production variables remains comparatively underdeveloped. The present study proposes an AI-assisted framework for integrating midgut digestive enzyme activity, gut microbiota and larval/cocoon traits in S. ricini. Three host-plant diets—Ricinus communis, Ailanthus altissima and Manihot esculenta—are considered within the proposed experimental framework. Digestive activities of α-amylase, protease, lipase and cellulase are proposed to be evaluated together with 16S rRNA-based bacterial community profiling. Larval growth, survival, cocoon weight, shell weight and shell percentage are incorporated as production-related variables. Statistical approaches including ANOVA, correlation analysis, diversity analysis and PERMANOVA are combined with machine-learning algorithms including Random Forest, XGBoost and Support Vector Regression. For methodological demonstration, a simulated dataset was constructed using biologically plausible ranges rather than experimental observations. The simulated analysis illustrates how integrated biochemical and microbial variables can be used to predict larval and cocoon performance and how SHAP-based explainable artificial intelligence can identify influential predictors. The framework suggests that microbiome–enzyme interactions may provide useful candidate biomarkers for future validation. However, simulated findings should not be interpreted as empirical evidence. The proposed framework provides a basis for future experimental studies aimed at microbiome-informed feeding, precision rearing and sustainable eri-silk production.

Abstract Environmental pollution is a complex and continuously evolving problem that requires rapid, sensitive and decentralized analytical technologies. Conventional analytical techniques such as atomic absorption spectrometry, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, gas chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography provide high analytical performance but generally require sophisticated instrumentation, laboratory infrastructure, sample preparation and trained personnel. Smart chemical sensors offer an attractive alternative because they can provide rapid measurements with portable and potentially low-cost instrumentation. However, environmental samples contain multiple interfering species, and sensor responses may be nonlinear, unstable or affected by temperature, pH, humidity and sensor ageing. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), provides new opportunities to overcome these limitations by extracting complex patterns from chemical-sensor responses and converting them into qualitative or quantitative information. This paper reviews the development of AI-driven smart chemical sensors for rapid environmental pollution detection, with emphasis on electrochemical sensors, gas-sensor arrays, optical sensors and nanomaterial-based sensing platforms. The application of machine-learning approaches including principal component analysis, support-vector machines, artificial neural networks, random forests and deep-learning models for signal processing, classification, quantification and sensor-drift compensation is discussed. Recent studies demonstrate the integration of deep learning, electrochemical sensing and Internet-of-Things technology for simultaneous detection of heavy metals in water. The paper also proposes an integrated framework combining chemical recognition, signal transduction, AI-based data interpretation, wireless communication and environmental decision support. Major challenges, including limited datasets, matrix effects, sensor drift, model interpretability and field validation, are discussed. AI-enabled chemical sensors have considerable potential to transform environmental monitoring from periodic laboratory analysis toward rapid, portable and intelligent pollution surveillance.

Abstract The escalating global demand for chemicals, materials, and energy has intensified concerns regarding resource depletion, hazardous waste generation, energy consumption, and environmental pollution. Green chemistry provides a sustainable paradigm by minimizing waste, reducing hazardous substances, improving energy efficiency, and promoting renewable resources. However, developing greener chemical processes traditionally requires extensive experimentation and optimization. Artificial intelligence (AI)—particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning, and predictive modeling—offers transformative opportunities to accelerate this transition. AI enables reaction prediction and optimization, catalyst discovery, green solvent selection, sustainable material design, toxicity prediction, waste minimization, and environmental monitoring by analyzing large chemical datasets and identifying relationships recognized through conventional approaches. Integration of AI with automation and advanced analytical techniques further enables faster, more efficient chemical research. This review discusses major applications of AI in green chemistry, emphasizing sustainable synthesis, catalysis, solvents, materials, waste management, energy technologies, and analytical chemistry. We address challenges associated with data quality, model interpretability, experimental validation, computational energy consumption, and industrial scale-up. Finally, we examine the potential of AI-driven green chemistry to support sustainable manufacturing, circular economy, resource efficiency, and technological innovation in India within the context of Viksit Bharat @2047. We conclude that integrating chemical expertise with AI provides a powerful pathway toward cleaner, safer, and more sustainable chemical technologies.

Abstract Agriculture is central to India's economic development, food security, rural employment, and the achievement of the Viksit Bharat@2047 vision. However, Indian agriculture faces increasingly complex challenges, including climate variability, water scarcity, soil degradation, pest and disease outbreaks, fragmented landholdings, market uncertainty, and unequal access to agricultural knowledge. These challenges require a transition from conventional, input-intensive agriculture towards data-driven, resource-efficient, climate-resilient and farmer-centric production systems. Agriculture in India is increasingly affected by climate variability, water scarcity, soil degradation, pest and disease outbreaks, and unpredictable weather conditions. These challenges threaten crop productivity and food security, particularly among small and marginal farmers. Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing, and machine learning offer new opportunities to transform conventional agricultural practices into data-driven precision agriculture systems. This paper presents a conceptual framework for AI-driven precision agriculture aimed at improving crop resilience under changing climatic conditions. Artificial Intelligence (AI), combined with precision agriculture, Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing, satellite imagery, drones, machine learning, robotics and digital public infrastructure, offers significant opportunities to transform Indian agriculture. AI can support crop and yield prediction, disease and pest identification, weather-based advisories, irrigation optimisation, soil management, crop insurance, market intelligence and early-warning systems. The paper also discusses challenges related to digital inclusion, data governance, affordability, AI reliability, farmer skills, privacy and institutional coordination. It argues that India's objective should not simply be the digitisation of agriculture, but the creation of an intelligent, inclusive and resilient agricultural ecosystem in which technology augments farmer knowledge and decision-making. By 2047, India can aspire to establish globally competitive agriculture that produces more with fewer resources, withstands climate shocks, generates higher and more stable farm incomes, and ensures sustainable food and nutritional security.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced materials are increasingly being integrated to accelerate research in sustainable energy technologies. This chapter examines the impact of artificial intelligence adoption on systemic risk in fintech-driven financial systems, emphasizing the need for integrated risk management, audit, and governance frameworks. The study develops a composite AI Risk Index using Principal Component Analysis to capture interactions between financial vulnerability, technological adoption, and institutional quality across 39 countries from 2010 to 2024 . Using fixed effects and dynamic panel GMM models alongside machine learning techniques, including Random Forest and SHAP explainability, the analysis identifies non-linear and threshold effects in the relationship between AI adoption and systemic risk. The findings show that AI can amplify systemic vulnerabilities beyond critical adoption levels, particularly in weak governance environments. The chapter also proposes a Risk–Audit–Governance framework and a risk zoning model, highlighting the importance of adaptive regulation, continuous auditing, and strong institutional capacity to ensure financial stability and accountability.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the modern workplace. Employers are increasingly using AI-enabled technologies to monitor attendance, productivity, communication, location, performance, behaviour and emotional responses of employees. While such technologies can offer advantages in terms of organisational efficiency, prevention of misconduct and management of large workforces, they also raise serious concerns over employee privacy, autonomy, dignity and labour rights. Traditional workplace monitoring was generally limited to physical observation, attendance registers and conventional electronic monitoring. AI has enabled wider collection of employee data, which is subsequently evaluated using automated systems. This research explores the relationship between AI-driven workplace surveillance and employee privacy rights, with reference to the Indian legal framework. It examines the challenges created by continuous monitoring, algorithmic decision-making, biometric surveillance, productivity tracking and employee profiling. The study argues that workplace surveillance should not be viewed solely as a question of managerial authority but should be addressed as a labour-rights and fundamental-rights issue. A balanced regulatory approach is therefore crucial to ensure that legitimate business interests do not override employee privacy and dignity. The research concludes with recommendations for transparency, proportionality, informed notice, data minimisation, human oversight and effective grievance mechanisms.

documents.abstract: Introduction Mental health difficulties among adolescents and youth (ages 10–24) are increasing globally, yet early intervention remains impeded by stigma, service shortages, and cultural barriers. AI-enabled technologies including chatbots, automated screening tools, and machine learning-based predictive models have been proposed as scalable approaches to address these gaps, alongside non-AI digital interventions such as therapist-guided internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) and smartphone-based CBT applications, which are examined as comparator evidence given their stronger controlled-design evidence base. Methods This scoping review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) reporting guidelines and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology. A systematic database search across six databases (PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, SpringerLink, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect), supplemented by manual and forward-citation searching, yielded 10,962 records, of which 19 studies met the predefined inclusion criteria. A Human-AI Collaboration Role framework comprising a four-level continuum from fully human-led to fully automated delivery was applied as a predefined coding dimension across all included studies. Results Most studies focused on depression and anxiety among mid-to-late adolescents in high-income countries (68.4%). Therapist-guided iCBT was the most rigorously studied format using randomized and controlled designs; AI chatbots, predictive models, and large language model (LLM)-based systems demonstrated feasibility or engagement outcomes in a limited number of studies and contexts, though randomized diagnostic chatbot trials specifically remain absent for participants under 18 years; at least one randomized non-diagnostic chatbot trial (a body-image intervention) has been conducted in this age group. Equity-related reporting was inconsistent: socioeconomic status was reported in only 10.5% of studies and cultural adaptation in 42.1%; restriction to English-language publications may further underrepresent non-Western and low- and middle-income-country evidence relevant to these equity findings. Key implementation challenges included inconsistent safeguarding protocols for minors, algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and insufficient integration with clinical and educational systems. Discussion The evidence base remains preliminary and methodologically heterogeneous, insufficient to support conclusions about clinical effectiveness or generalizability to diverse adolescent populations. These findings represent a descriptive map of the current evidence landscape rather than an assessment of effectiveness. Future research should prioritize adequately powered adolescent-focused trials, participatory co-design approaches, culturally informed adaptations, and transparent ethical governance frameworks to ensure responsible development of AI-enabled digital mental health tools for youth. Because the included studies were heterogeneous and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was undertaken, this review does not establish comparative clinical effectiveness, safety, or superiority of AI-enabled interventions. documents.abstract: Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into performance appraisal systems has fundamentally transformed how organizations evaluate, reward, and guide talent. This paper examines the complex interplay between automated machine feedback, employee intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and long-term career mobility within modern corporate structures. Traditional performance reviews, historically plagued by manager bias, infrequent feedback cycles, and administrative lag, are increasingly being replaced by real-time, algorithmic evaluation tools that continuously monitor productivity, communication patterns, and milestone attainment. While these advanced systems offer unprecedented objectivity, data granularity, and operational efficiency, they simultaneously introduce critical psychological and structural challenges for the workforce. The research investigates how algorithmic oversight impacts employee motivation, exploring the fine line between constructive data-driven guidance and dehumanizing surveillance. When machine feedback is perceived as opaque, overly punitive, or devoid of contextual empathy, it can trigger algorithmic anxiety, disengagement, and strategic gaming of metrics. Conversely, when integrated transparently, AI-driven insights can empower employees with actionable developmental pathways, aligning daily performance with overarching career trajectories. The study further analyzes the implications of automated career mobility, evaluating how machine-generated talent mapping influences promotions, skill-gap identification, and succession planning. It highlights the risk of algorithmic bias reinforcing historical inequities, thereby restricting advancement opportunities for diverse employee segments if human oversight is absent. Methodologically, this paper synthesizes contemporary organizational psychology literature with a comparative evaluation of organizations deploying AI-augmented human resource management systems. The analytical framework correlates the frequency and framing of machine feedback with metrics of employee retention, morale, and promotional velocity. The findings suggest that optimal performance outcomes are achieved not through pure automation, but through a hybrid model where AI serves as an objective diagnostic tool that amplifies—rather than replaces—human managerial mentorship and empathy. Ultimately, this study provides human resource leaders and technologists with a strategic framework for designing ethical, motivation-enhancing appraisal architectures that foster sustainable career growth and organizational agility.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has transformed visual art, raising questions about authenticity, creativity, and authorship. This chapter examines how authenticity is redefined in AI-generated imagery by integrating perspectives from aesthetics, creativity studies, and AI research. It proposes a process-oriented framework in which authenticity is understood as a relational and context-dependent construct emerging from interactions between human creators, algorithms, and audiences. Generative AI challenges traditional notions of originality by introducing distributed creative agency, while lacking intentionality behind its outputs. Human–AI collaboration shifts artistic practice from manual execution to conceptual direction, curation, and interpretation. Audience perceptions of authenticity are shaped not only by visual quality but also by knowledge of production processes. The chapter argues that authenticity is not diminished but transformed, requiring new frameworks and stronger emphasis on transparency, trust, and responsible governance.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is changing how consumers search for, evaluate and use information in digital marketplaces. One emerging application is the use of AI-generated review summaries, which condense large volumes of online consumer reviews into concise statements about product strengths, weaknesses and frequently mentioned attributes. Such summaries can reduce information overload and improve search efficiency, but they also raise concerns regarding credibility, transparency, objectivity, selective omission and consumer reliance on machine-generated interpretations of peer opinions. This study examines AI-generated review summaries and their potential influence on purchase decisions among Indian Gen Z consumers. The study is primarily secondary-research-led and synthesises recent literature on AI-mediated electronic word-of-mouth, review credibility, transparency, trust and perceived diagnosticity. To complement the secondary evidence, an exploratory primary survey of 120 respondents collected through Google Forms is incorporated as an empirical component. The study adopts the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) perspective and signalling theory to structure the relationships among perceived transparency, perceived usefulness, perceived objectivity, consumer trust, perceived diagnosticity and purchase intention. The paper proposes that trust and diagnosticity function as important mechanisms through which characteristics of AI-generated review summaries can influence purchase intention. The empirical component is designed to provide descriptive and exploratory evidence rather than to replace the broader secondary research base. Statistical analysis includes respondent profiling, descriptive statistics, reliability assessment, correlation analysis and appropriate hypothesis testing, subject to the structure of the 120-response dataset. The study contributes to understanding how AI-mediated review information can support consumer decision-making while highlighting the importance of transparency, balanced representation and access to original reviews.

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications have driven education toward more adaptive and personalized learning experiences and environments. By offering educators tools to customize learning paths, adapt resources to students’ needs, and provide tailored feedback, AI applications are able to boost student academic achievement and motivation. This study seeks to assess the impact of an AI-enhanced learning approach on students’ academic achievement and motivation. We employed a quasi-experimental method for this study with a total of 54 sixth-grade pupils at a private bilingual school in Barka, Oman split into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group was taught using AI applications and the control group was taught using the Moodle learning management system. Results of the study indicate that the AI-powered approach significantly increased students’ academic achievement (p < .05) and motivation (p < .01), with notable gains in attention, confidence, and relevance. ’The findings of the study highlight the significant potential of AI to reshape learners’ experiences and enhance learning and motivation by providing adaptive and personalized learning. Given the small sample size and study environment, the generalizability of the results is limited. Future studies should investigate the scalability of AI-powered learning aids across different educational environments.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now drives core corporate decision, such as loan approvals and hiring screens, yet corporate boards have largely treated its governance as a management-level policy questions rather than a fiduciary obligation. This paper argues that this framing is mistaken, using Delaware's Caremark doctrine, as refined by Marchand v. Barnhill, In re Boeing, and In re McDonald's. The relevant cases already impose an enforceable duty on boards to actively oversee mission algorithmic systems, and by applying Marchand's mission-critical standard, this paper demonstrates that AI performs core business functions that expose companies to anti-discrimination, consumer protection, and securities liability. The paper also identifies a structural problem that existing doctrine has not confronted: unlike the legible red flags at issue in Caremark, Boeing, and Clovis Oncology, AI systems generate outputs without human-readable explanations, allowing boards to receive clean compliance reports from systems that are producing unlawful outcomes. This "black box problem" requires reestablishing what good-faith oversight demands and when the underlying risk bypasses traditional reporting structures. Drawing on In re SolarWinds and the officer liability extension in McDonald's, this paper proposes a scalable framework for reasonable AI oversight, including board-level AI audit committees, a Chief AI Officer role with reporting duties to the General Counsel and CEO, mandatory governance disclosure, and a safe harbor for compliance. Ultimately, this paper challenges that the doctrinal tools to govern AI already exist within Delaware law, and all that remains is for boards to act before litigation forces the question.

documents.abstract: Platform economies are reorganising the everyday conditions through which urban residents feel connected, isolated, or at home. Discussions of gig work typically begin with flexibility and income, overlooking how apps, ratings, incentives, and algorithmic decisions reshape the social setting of work itself. This chapter argues that urban loneliness should be understood not only as a private feeling but as an outcome shaped by how work, time, and urban space are organised. Drawing on social capital theory, economic sociology, urban studies, and research on algorithmic management, the chapter develops a conceptual framework explaining how platform design weakens some forms of social connection while enabling new forms of worker solidarity. The discussion considers how these dynamics intersect with gender, psychological strain, and migrant status. Cases from Uber, Ola, Urban Company, Indian delivery platforms, New York City, Seattle, the European Union, and India's social-security framework illustrate these dynamics in practice.

Background As organizations embed algorithmic agents in operations, alignment is presumed to make human–AI teams safer and more effective. Yet it leaves the orientation of alignment unexamined, that is, what humans and agents actually coordinate around. Objective Drawing on bricolage theory, this study distinguishes three orientations of alignment: tangible-resource, opportunity-oriented, and risk-oriented, then examines how each relates to collaborative fluency and to financial and inventory risk. Methods We analyzed 141 simulated supply-chain teams, each pairing a human manager with seven rule-based AI agents between 24 and 47 cycles. Behavioral logs were coded for alignment orientation, while collaborative fluency, risk behavior and outcomes were computed from logs by hierarchical regression. Results Tangible-resource alignment was associated with lower inventory redundancy and smaller drawdown. Risk-oriented alignment was associated with greater net-asset volatility and drawdown, associations that weakened once financing was controlled. Opportunity-oriented alignment showed no associations. No orientation explained collaborative fluency, and financing dominated financial risk. Conclusions Whether human–AI alignment reduces risk depends on its orientation. Tangible-resource alignment can buffer operational risk, but risk-oriented alignment may mark risk-taking rather than control it. Effective teaming depends less on more alignment than on aligning in right domain, with restraint in financing as the primary safeguard.
