documents.abstract: Background: Longitudinal policy research requires measures of what policy applied, when, and with what provisions, yet government sources are organized and preserved in ways that can make historical policy difficult to reconstruct. This study developed and evaluated an end-to-end workflow for constructing longitudinal policy measures from government web sources.Methods: The workflow was applied to NHS England’s Additional Roles Reimbursement Scheme (ARRS), a national policy specifying which primary-care workforce categories are eligible for reimbursement, from 2019/20 to 2026/27. It combined historical document recovery, variable specification, automated extraction against a human-coded reference standard, and longitudinal measure construction. Keyword, deterministic, and large language model (LLM) methods were compared across eight development and six later evaluation versions. Three simplified measurement strategies were compared with the author-verified longitudinal reference. Exploratory source recovery assessments were also conducted in Spain, France, and Australia.Results: Historical reconstruction identified 14 substantive document versions across eight policy years, including within-year changes in reimbursement eligibility, amounts, and conditions. Reimbursable primary-care workforce categories increased from 5 to 27, while the current NHS England landing page provided access to documents from only one policy year. On the six later evaluation versions, the LLM matched all scored reference-standard targets for eligibility status, effective dates, and reimbursement amounts, although eligibility conditions remained more difficult to extract. Simplified measurement strategies changed the reconstructed policy history. Using only the current specification could not recover historical eligibility, one specification per policy year assigned 96 eligible category-months (7.3%) too early, and keyword coding produced 138 category-month errors (10.5%).Conclusion: Valid longitudinal policy measurement requires historical reconstruction, explicit variable and dating rules, evaluation on later documents, and human verification. For health-politics research, this approach can support measures of changing governmental choices about eligibility, financing, conditions, and timing while distinguishing formal policy from implementation and outcomes.

ABSTRACT Biochemistry education faces persistent challenges in equipping students with the skills required to manage complex laboratory protocols, advanced instrumentation, and analytical procedures, particularly in high‐risk or resource‐intensive experimental settings. Traditional hands‐on training is constrained by limited access to equipment, safety concerns, and high operational costs, hindering institutions from providing realistic and scalable laboratory experiences. However, Digital Twin technology presents a transformative alternative. It creates simulations of real biochemical laboratories, providing immersive, scalable, and cost‐efficient environments unconstrained by physical limitations. This approach supports interactive, avatar‐mediated engagement that bridges conceptual knowledge with applied practice. In this study, we aimed to introduce BioDTLab, a custom Digital Twin framework for biochemistry education that integrates Virtual Reality, Internet of Things, robotics, data analytics, and an Artificial Intelligence (AI)‐driven Virtual Chat‐GPT Tutor. BioDTLab synchronizes physical and digital domains to provide high‐fidelity simulations of biochemical processes and instrumentation, while the AI‐driven Virtual Chat‐GPT Tutor evaluates student engagement, comprehension, and procedural accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that Digital Twin frameworks, such as BioDTLab, can redefine biochemistry education by making advanced experiential learning more accessible, safe, and scalable, while reducing reliance on costly physical resources. BioDTLab integrates immersive simulation, real‐time data synchronization, and AI‐driven feedback to provide a sustainable model for future science education that enhances conceptual understanding and practical competence. In addition, its adaptability makes it suitable for instructional models, such as the flipped classroom, where pre‐laboratory virtual practice can complement and enhance in‐person laboratory training.

Abstract India's higher education system has never lacked policy mandates for community engagement. What it has consistently lacked is a working mechanism to connect community-identified problems with academic institutions positioned to address them. This paper proposes the Integrated Community Engagement & Project Management System (ICEPMS) — a single-window digital ecosystem that bridges this gap by linking community demand directly to higher education delivery. The paper develops a five-stakeholder conceptual model through systematic analysis of national policy documents, international frameworks, and established scholarship on community-based participatory research (CBPR) and service-learning. The proposed system enables citizens, Gram Panchayat members, NGOs, and journalists to report local problems digitally; allows administrators to convert those problems into credit-mapped academic topics; enables colleges and students to execute Community Engagement Projects; records performance transparently; and facilitates funding from CSR departments and government officers based on verifiable institutional performance. The paper discusses the role of artificial intelligence as a supportive accelerator within the system. ICEPMS aligns with the mandates of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, the UGC Guidelines for Fostering Social Responsibility and Community Engagement in Higher Education Institutions in India 2.0 (2022), and institutional Community Engagement Project frameworks. By providing operational infrastructure for existing policy intent, the paper contributes a practical framework for community engagement in Indian higher education.

An Integrated Computer Vision and Machine Learning Framework for Sorghum Disease Severity Assessment and Yield Prediction presents a technology-driven approach for automated crop health monitoring and yield estimation in sorghum cultivation. The study integrates computer vision techniques and machine learning algorithms to identify and quantify disease severity from crop images and to predict potential yield based on relevant visual and agronomic characteristics. The framework aims to reduce the limitations of conventional manual disease assessment, which can be time-consuming and subject to human variability. Image processing and feature extraction techniques are employed to capture disease-related characteristics, while machine learning models support classification, severity estimation, and yield prediction. By combining disease assessment with yield forecasting, the proposed framework provides a comprehensive approach to precision agriculture and data-driven crop management. The work demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence and computer vision to support timely decision-making, improve crop monitoring, and contribute to sustainable and efficient sorghum production.

This paper presents the design, development, and evaluation of a human-centric smart mental environment that integrates internet of things (IoT)-enabled sensors and artificial intelligence (AI) for the early detection of adolescent mental health indicators. Adolescent mental health disorders, including stress, anxiety, and depression, are increasingly prevalent yet remain underdiagnosed due to reliance on subjective self-reports and clinical interviews. Early detection is critical but hindered by symptom underreporting and the absence of continuous, objective monitoring tools suitable for real-world environments. To address this gap, the proposed system captures three complementary modalities: (1) facial expression features using a front-facing camera, (2) body motion and acceleration patterns using a wearable accelerometer and gyroscope, and (3) postural pressure distribution using an eight-element pressure array positioned along the thoracic and lumbar regions. Multimodal data are preprocessed using temporal-spatial filtering, followed by a cross-modal attention-based fusion mechanism that dynamically weights the most informative modality within each time window. A supervised learning classifier then predicts four mental states: normal, stress, anxiety, and depression. The system was evaluated using a dataset collected from 64 adolescents aged 14–18 under semi-natural, classroom-like conditions. The proposed attention-based multimodal framework achieved an overall classification accuracy of 89.2%, significantly outperforming unimodal baselines (facial-only: 77.8%, motion-only: 74.5%, posture-only: 71.3%) and simple concatenation fusion (83.5%). The attention mechanism improved the classification F1-score to 0.88 and demonstrated robustness under lighting and posture variations. Statistical analysis confirmed the superiority of the multimodal approach (p < 0.01). The system provides a non-invasive, scalable, and human-centric solution for continuous adolescent mental health monitoring, with strong potential for deployment in schools and community health programs.

Anal dysplasia is the precursor of most anal squamous cell carcinomas and represents the central target of contemporary anal cancer prevention. Increasing recognition of high-risk populations, together with a better understanding of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated carcinogenesis and the results of the Anal Cancer/HSIL Outcomes Research (ANCHOR) trial, has shifted the focus from detecting disease to preventing cancer through the identification and treatment of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL). This chapter reviews the current concepts underlying anal dysplasia, including its epidemiology, natural history, risk factors, pathogenesis, histopathologic classification, diagnostic evaluation, and available therapeutic strategies. Particular emphasis is placed on the transition from the traditional anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) classification to the Lower Anogenital Squamous Terminology (LAST) system, the pivotal role of high-resolution anoscopy with directed biopsy as the diagnostic reference standard, and the evidence supporting contemporary screening and treatment algorithms. Prevention is discussed as a continuum encompassing HPV vaccination, sexual health interventions, HIV prevention and treatment, early detection of HSIL, and long-term surveillance after therapy. Finally, the chapter highlights current challenges, including the need for standardized HRA training, development of centers of excellence, and international collaborative research to improve implementation, validate emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and precision risk prediction, and ultimately expand access to effective anal cancer prevention worldwide.

The article highlights the mismatch between existing design approaches and the conditions of modern combat operations, as reliability assessment is often conducted only for individual factors in isolation. Based on the system analysis, the authors identified and classified three main groups of influencing factors: natural (meteorological conditions, geophysical factors, and physical effects), anthropogenic (combat conditions, man-made interference, and the human factor), and technical (hardware, information-processing and algorithmic, and dynamic factors). Their components and the nature of each factor’s impact on the aircraft control system are described in detail. Based on the results of the analysis, three detailed structural-hierarchical diagrams of the influencing factors have been developed. The generalized structural-hierarchical framework allows for a comprehensive consideration of internal and external threats that arise throughout the entire aircraft lifecycle and directly affect combat employment effectiveness. The authors substantiate that the reliability and operational effectiveness of an aircraft control system must be considered as equivalent and interrelated characteristics. The created structural-hierarchical framework will serve as a foundation for the subsequent determination of the minimum necessary set of properties that modern and prospective aircraft control systems must possess.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare, particularly in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of diagnostic medical imaging and radiotherapy has witnessed significant advancements, revolutionizing the healthcare landscape. This review delves into its diverse applications, exploring its potential to boost accuracy, streamline workflows, and improve patient outcomes. A systematic literature search identified relevant studies on AI's role in these domains. Articles covered topics like image analysis, pattern recognition, decision support, and treatment planning. AI algorithms, performance, and integration into clinical practice were critically evaluated. In diagnostic imaging, AI shines in modalities like MRI, CT, and PET. AI algorithms excel in image interpretation, aiding early detection, characterization, and staging of various diseases. Additionally, these tools show promise in predicting treatment response and personalizing treatment plans. Within radiotherapy, AI automates and improves treatment steps. Machine learning algorithms efficiently contour target volumes and organs at risk, facilitating optimal treatment planning. Real-time image guidance and AI-driven adaptive radiotherapy techniques enhance precision and safety during treatment delivery. Moreover, AI-based predictive models assist in assessing outcomes and optimizing therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving patient care. Despite the advancements, challenges like data privacy, standardization, and ethical considerations persist. This review paints a comprehensive picture of AI's current applications in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy, highlighting its transformative impact on disease diagnosis and treatment planning. As AI evolves, its integration into clinical practice holds immense potential to revolutionize patient care, ushering in a new era of precision medicine.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have substantially advanced natural language generation (NLG), but high-quality content creation remains constrained by hallucination, limited controllability, retrieval noise, domain shift, and computational cost. This study proposes Retrieval-Augmented and Preference-Aligned Generation (RAP-Gen), a unified framework that integrates retrieval-augmented generation, factual preference alignment, in-context learning, and denoising pre-training. The framework combines a dense semantic retriever with an encoder–decoder generator, introduces pairwise factual-preference supervision for controllable generation, aligns retrieval and generation distributions, and uses structured text corruption to improve robustness to incomplete or noisy inputs. Experiments are reported on summarization, long-form creative writing, and knowledge-intensive question answering using CNN/DailyMail, WritingPrompts, Natural Questions, and general language-modeling data. The reported results show that RAP-Gen improves ROUGE, BERTScore, perplexity, FactScore, and human-rated factuality relative to the baselines listed in the manuscript. Ablation results indicate that removing retrieval, preference alignment, or denoising degrades performance, supporting the complementary roles of external knowledge, preference signals, and robust pre-training. Additional analyses examine the number of retrieved documents, attention over retrieved evidence, robustness under input perturbation, model scaling, and in-context learning. Because the supplied material does not include raw predictions, code, repeated-run variance, annotator agreement statistics, or complete benchmark configurations, the numerical results are interpreted as reported experimental outcomes rather than independently reproducible evidence. The study contributes an integrated design for knowledge-grounded, preference-aware content generation and identifies evaluation and reproducibility requirements for future work.

Manufacturing workplaces involve hazards associated with machinery, material handling, worker practices, and environmental conditions. This study aimed to assess occupational health and safety conditions and identify priorities for improvement at a water fixture component manufacturing facility in Istanbul, Türkiye. A descriptive assessment was conducted using the ELMERI Observation Method across seven categories. A single researcher conducted observations three days per week from April to June 2021 and recorded 114 checklist-item ratings, comprising 74 correct and 40 incorrect classifications. Category-specific and overall safety indices were calculated from these counts. The overall index was 64.9%. Safety-related behavior had the highest category index (83.3%), followed by first aid and fire safety (71.4%), order and cleanliness (68.4%), and machine safety (66.7%). Lower indices were obtained for ergonomics (50.0%), industrial hygiene (44.4%), and floors and passageways (25.0%). The findings indicate that favorable ratings for observed worker practices coexisted with deficiencies in physical workplace conditions. Priorities included unobstructed passageways, machine guarding, ventilation, and ergonomic improvements. Unequal observation counts, potential observer bias, and the single-facility design limit interpretation and generalizability. The assessment identified practical priorities for the facility; the effectiveness of the proposed corrective actions requires follow-up evaluation.

Dual probabilistic linguistic term sets (DPLTSs) provide a powerful tool for describing uncertain, hesitant, and bipolar linguistic assessments in complex decision-making settings. Current aggregation methods for dual probabilistic linguistic information still have drawbacks. They can hardly mitigate the interference brought by biased assessment values and fail to capture the correlations among arbitrary attributes. To address these limitations, this paper develops a new class of dual probabilistic linguistic Archimedean power Muirhead mean (DPLAPMM) operators for multipleattribute decision making (MADM). First, by combining the advantages of Archimedean triangular norms with the power Muirhead mean (PMM) operator, the DPLAPMM operator together with its weighted form are developed. The proposed operators can reduce the impact of unreasonable evaluation values while modeling the interrelationships among any number of attributes. Then, a dual probabilistic linguistic entropy is constructed to obtain objective attribute weights, which are combined with subjective weights to generate comprehensive attribute weights. Based on these results, a MADM method is established under a dual probabilistic linguistic environment. An illustrative case concerning industrial artificial intelligence (AI) project selection is used to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method, and comparative analyses show its flexibility and effectiveness over existing approaches.

Agentic artificial intelligence can improve Internet of Things (IoT) workflow resilience by reasoning over runtime context and generating recovery plans across devices, edge gateways, cloud services, and enterprise applications. However, autonomously completed recovery actions may still violate authorization, privacy, data-residency, actuator-safety, cost, or operational constraints. This paper proposes ARPE-IoT, an Adaptive Recovery and Policy Enforcement Framework for Agentic IoT Workflows. ARPE-IoT treats agent-generated recovery actions as proposals that must pass hard runtime policies before execution. Permissible actions are ranked using soft operational utility, executed under a bounded recovery budget, validated against workflow and physical-state conditions, audited, and escalated to humans when autonomous resolution is unsafe. We implemented a lightweight Python simulator with temperature and occupancy sensors, two edge gateways, two cloud services, an HVAC actuator, a policy engine, and a constrained recovery planner. Across 10,800 simulated executions covering normal operation and eight injected failure classes, ARPE-IoT achieved a 100% safe handling rate, consisting of 82.2% autonomous resolution and 17.8% controlled safe-state escalation. It reduced policy violations from 22.2% for unconstrained agents and 33.3% for rule-based recovery to 0% in the evaluated scenarios, with 47.7 ms mean latency.

Abstract The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into daily life is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of human social interaction and communication patterns. AI-powered tools, from sophisticated chatbots and virtual assistants to complex social media algorithms, are increasingly mediating, augmenting, and, in some cases, replacing human-to-human communication. This paper explores the transformative impact of AI on how people connect, express emotions, and form relationships. We examine the dual nature of this shift, highlighting the benefits of enhanced efficiency, accessibility, and personalization, while also scrutinizing the profound risks, including the potential for social isolation, the erosion of authentic connection, the creation of algorithmic echo chambers, and ethical challenges such as bias and lack of transparency. Ultimately, the paper argues that navigating the future of social interaction requires a critical balance between embracing AI's capabilities and prioritizing the core human values of empathy, connection, and ethical accountability.

documents.abstract: Introduction Strategic and organizational solutions are becoming essential due to the global demand for digital transformation, sustained operational efficiency, and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence adoption on organizational efficiency, with digital literacy as a boundary condition and organizational learning capability serving as a mediator. Methods The study utilized a quantitative cross-sectional survey-based design. A multistage sampling technique was used to collect data from employees working in the Ghanaian banking sector. Data collected from 388 employees from the banks were utilized in an empirical study employing structural equation modeling. Both direct and indirect relationships were assessed. Results The findings revealed that the level of artificial intelligence adoption has a significant and positive influence on both organizational efficiency and organizational learning capability. The results further showed that organizational learning capability has a significant and positive influence on organizational efficiency and partially mediates the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency. Additionally, the results revealed that digital literacy moderates the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency, as well as the relationships between organizational learning capability and organizational efficiency. Conclusion This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that connects the hitherto overlooked linkages between artificial intelligence adoption, organizational learning capability, digital literacy, and organizational efficiency within the banking sector of an emerging economy. By integrating these constructs into a unified model, the study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI adoption translates into organizational efficiency, thereby extending the Resource-Based View in an emerging-market context.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing audit practice by expanding analytical coverage, automating routine procedures, and supporting more continuous risk assessment. These benefits, however, also raise questions about accountability, explainability, professional judgment, data protection, and legal responsibility. This study examines whether AI auditability and oversight design shape assurance professionals’ perceptions of ethical risk, legal exposure, and audit quality in Ghana. Using a quantitative design, the study combines a cross-sectional survey of 180 assurance professionals with a between-subjects vignette experiment. AI auditability was assessed in terms of data traceability, model documentation, explainability, governance controls, role clarity, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) procedures. The experiment compared manual-only auditing, AI-only auditing, and AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. AI auditability was negatively associated with perceived ethical risk (β = −0.456, p < .001) and positively associated with perceived audit quality (β = 0.424, p < .001). Perceived ethical risk was positively associated with perceived legal exposure (β = 0.536, p < .001) and negatively associated with perceived audit quality (β = −0.268, p < .001). Although AI auditability was negatively correlated with perceived legal exposure, its direct regression effect was not statistically significant after ethical risk was controlled (β = −0.092, p = .392). The experiment showed that AI-only oversight was associated with higher perceptions of ethical and legal risk than AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. Because the study measures professional perceptions rather than observed legal events or realized audit outcomes, the findings should be interpreted as evidence about perceived risk and quality. Overall, the results indicate that responsible AI adoption in auditing depends less on automation alone than on auditable governance, meaningful human oversight, and clear accountability.

documents.abstract: Abstract In the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the field of Library and Information Science is evolving rapidly with the introduction of new paradigms in information management, information discovery, and service delivery. This is a conceptual paper that analyses the role of AI and its future implications on the library and information services. It examines key AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, chatbots, robotics, AI-powered discovery services, personalized information services and generative AI, and explores how these are being used in modern libraries. This paper emphasises the benefits of these technologies in information retrieval, automating repetitive library functions, delivering personalized services to users, facilitating research activities, and engaging users. It also looks at how technology is evolving like smart libraries and AI-driven information services. Meanwhile, the paper covers important challenges that must be addressed in the context of the adoption of AI, such as privacy, data security, algorithmic bias, misinformation, copyright, ethical issues, technological costs, and technical skills. The evolving nature of the role of LIS professionals and the skills needed to collaborate with emerging AI technologies are given special attention. The paper proposes that AI is not the end of librarians but an enabler and a supportive tool for librarians. By combining AI with professional knowledge, ethical considerations, and human-centred services, libraries can become smarter, more efficient, user-friendly, and responsive to user needs. The study highlights the need for responsible use of AI, ongoing professional growth, and collaboration between technology and human skills to shape the future of library services. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an established part of how organizations run their operations, from customer interaction and demand forecasting to logistics, marketing, and knowledge work. This paper examines what that means for global business operations through a documentary case study of Amazon. The study does not collect primary data or measure Amazon's performance independently. It analyzes publicly available sources: Amazon's corporate publications and regulatory filings, reports from international institutions, and peer-reviewed research. The paper keeps a clear line between what Amazon reports having deployed and what independent evidence shows about outcomes. The paper finds that AI can support productivity, personalization, forecasting, automation, and human decision support, but that the effects are neither automatic nor uniform. Drawing on independent studies, it notes that productivity gains can be substantial for some workers, particularly less-experienced ones, while AI can reduce performance on tasks outside its effective capability range. Amazon illustrates how AI can be integrated across a value chain, including recommendations, fulfilment and robotics, demand forecasting, and generative-AI services. The case also shows why adoption needs governance, workforce development, data management, risk assessment, and human oversight. The paper concludes with an eight-step framework for responsible enterprise AI adoption. It starts from a defined business problem, evaluates AI at the level of individual tasks, and draws on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for risk management. It argues that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on organizational readiness and the quality of human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI and ML are rapidly changing higher education by redefining teaching, learning, research, evaluation, and institutional governance. India's National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions a transdisciplinary, technology-enabled, learner-centric, and innovation-driven education system that produces globally competent graduates who can contribute to Viksit Bharat 2047. Despite rising acceptance of AI-based educational technology, equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, digital infrastructure, and curriculum revision for future workforce needs remain problems. This study critically investigates how AI and ML might improve the quality, accessibility, inclusivity, and effectiveness of higher education in India within NEP 2020. It examines the transformative potential of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, predictive learning analytics, automated assessment, academic administration, and research support, using a doctrinal and analytical research methodology grounded in policy documents, government reports, and contemporary academic literature. It also highlights algorithmic unfairness, data privacy, cybersecurity, digital inequality, academic integrity, and ethical issues in the implementation of generative AI. The Competency-Based AI Integration Framework (AI-HE 2047 Framework) integrates digital literacy, critical thinking, interdisciplinary learning, research and innovation, ethical AI governance, and lifelong learning competencies to align AI adoption with the goals of NEP 2020. The methodology helps higher education institutions produce AI-ready graduates for an innovation-driven knowledge economy. The study found that responsible integration of AI and ML, supported by policy reforms, faculty capacity building, institutional readiness, and ethical governance mechanisms, can improve educational quality, employability, research excellence, and India's transition to a knowledge-powered economy under Viksit Bharat 2047.

documents.abstract: Abstract Patents Act drafted in 1970 for a world of mechanical assemblies and chemical formulations and then has to stretch them, sometimes uncomfortably, to fit technologies nobody anticipated. Artificial intelligence is the latest and perhaps the most demanding of these stretches. It is central to the country’s Viksit Bharat @2047 ambitions, driving growth in pharmaceuticals, semiconductor design, fintech, and advanced manufacturing, yet it sits awkwardly within a patent regime built on the presumption that an inventor is a natural person who can be named, questioned, and held accountable. This paper works through three points of friction between AI and Indian patent law, testing each against how comparable jurisdictions the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Patent Office have responded. The first is inventorship itself: whether a system such as DABUS can ever satisfy Sections 2(1)(y) and 6 of the Patents Act, 1970, and what happens to applications where a human contributor is named largely as a matter of convenience rather than genuine authorship. The second is the Section 3(k) exclusion for computer programmes per se and algorithms, read alongside the Delhi High Court’s technical-effect reasoning in Ferid Allani and its later application to AI-adjacent claims. The third concerns disclosure: what Section 10(4) can realistically demand of a model whose internal decision pathway is, by design, not fully interpretable even to the people who trained it. Rather than treat these as abstract doctrinal puzzles, the paper closes with a set of concrete, implementable proposals clarified guidance on human-contribution thresholds, an updated CRI examination manual with AI-specific illustrations, a Budapest-Treaty-style depository for training artefacts, and time-limited sui generis right for genuinely autonomous outputs. The underlying argument is a modest one: India does not need to choose between protecting human ingenuity and encouraging AI-driven research. It needs sharper definitions, and it needs them before the volume of AI-related filings makes ad hoc case-by-case resolution unworkable.

This book review critically examines Ekaterina Glebova's Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in the Sports Industry: Past, Present, and Future (CRC Press, 2026) through the lens of AI implementation management. While the book offers a timely and accessible overview of AI applications across coaching, athlete training, fan engagement, and stadium operations, it suffers from several fundamental limitations that reduce its utility for implementation-focused scholars and practitioners. This review identifies five critical gaps: (1) the absence of a political economy perspective on how AI reinforces existing power asymmetries; (2) neglect of non-elite sports and the digital divide; (3) oversimplification of organizational resistance and human-AI conflict; (4) reliance on non-peer-reviewed sources and lack of empirical evidence; and (5) raising ethical questions without providing actionable answers. The review concludes that the book serves as a valuable starting point for early-stage AI adoption but fails to offer step-by-step implementation frameworks, lessons from failures, or concrete guidance for resource-constrained organizations. For researchers contributing to this special issue on AI implementation, this review highlights critical directions for future inquiry, including maturity models, ROI measurement frameworks, and empirical studies of genuine implementation failures.

documents.abstract: BackgroundKnowledge sharing and digitally enabled workplace practices can promote environmentally sustainable behaviour in healthcare organisations. However, limited research has examined how smart workplace practices transmit the effects of knowledge sharing on green learning and green employee voice.ObjectiveThis study investigates the effects of knowledge sharing on green learning and green employee voice and examines the mediating role of artificial intelligence enabled workplace practices in these relationships.MethodsA positivist, quantitative design was adopted. Data were collected from 1954 professionals employed in private hospitals in emerging country and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling and Necessary Condition Analysis.ResultsKnowledge sharing had significant positive effects on green learning (β = 0.469, p < 0.001), green employee voice (β = 0.455, p < 0.001), and smart workplace practices (β = 0.594, p < 0.001). Smart workplace practices partially mediated the effects of knowledge sharing on green learning (indirect β = 0.249, p < 0.001) and green employee voice (indirect β = 0.271, p < 0.001). The model explained 62.9% of the variance in green learning and 66.2% in green employee voice. Necessary Condition Analysis also identified knowledge sharing as a necessary condition for achieving these green outcomes.ConclusionsKnowledge sharing facilitates green learning and employee voice both directly and through smart workplace practices. Healthcare managers should integrate knowledge-sharing mechanisms with smart workplace systems to cultivate environmentally responsible learning and communication behaviours.

Abstract The continuing advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for higher education and academic library development. The increasing volume of digital information, expansion of online education, and growing complexity of scholarly communication require libraries to provide faster, more responsive, and user-oriented information services. AI can assist academic libraries in areas such as intelligent discovery of scholarly resources, automated reference assistance, resource recommendation, metadata creation, research support, collection analysis, and digital preservation. This paper examines the emerging applications of AI in academic libraries and considers how these developments can support the broader objectives of Viksit Bharat@2047. Particular attention is given to the advantages of AI as well as concerns involving accuracy, privacy, copyright, ethics, infrastructure, digital inequality, and professional competencies. The paper argues that AI should function as an enabling technology rather than a substitute for librarians. The combination of computational capabilities with professional knowledge and human judgement can transform academic libraries into more responsive centres for learning, research, innovation, and knowledge sharing. Properly implemented AI-based library services can therefore strengthen the contribution of academic libraries to quality education, research capacity, digital literacy, and inclusive access to knowledge, thereby supporting India's long-term development aspirations.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are entering accredited conformity assessment, where the competence of assessors, auditors, inspectors, laboratory personnel and decision-makers is a constitutive element of confidence in the result. This article examines the risk of deskilling: deterioration, or insufficient maintenance, of task-specific independent professional capability through cognitive offloading, automation bias and overreliance. The argument rests on existing competence-maintenance requirements, domain-general evidence on offloading and automation bias, and experimental evidence on AI-assisted documentary reasoning and on skill formation when decision aids are withdrawn; clinical deskilling studies are treated as peripheral corroboration. The analysis examines the normative documents of the eleven Global ACI MRA scopes together with ISO/IEC 17011, ISO 19011, ISO/IEC 42001/42006, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended in 2026, and current accreditation-body guidance. Across these instruments competence, authorisation and accountability are assigned to persons and bodies, while AI is governed through validation, monitoring, security and human-oversight controls; none establishes AI as competent conformity-assessment personnel. Because many conformity-assessment judgements have no single external ground truth, erosion of independent reasoning may not be exposed by plausible output. The article argues that AI may substitute for tasks but cannot fulfil roles reserved to competent persons; distinguishes augmenting uses, through which accumulated expertise is exercised, from substituting uses, through which it is drawn down; proposes functional analogues of the established impartiality threats for human–machine interaction; and observes that interaction with a tool lacks the human friction through which competence is formed. Six proportionate safeguards and a research agenda are proposed. Direct longitudinal evidence in this population remains limited; the article therefore advances a risk-based competence-management argument, not a claim that deskilling has been demonstrated. The governing principle is that AI should augment professional competence, not become its source.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across anesthesiology and intensive care medicine (ICM), where complex data, continuous monitoring, and time-sensitive decisions create substantial opportunities for computational decision support. However, the clinical readiness of many AI applications remains uncertain. Methods: This narrative review provides a structured and clinically oriented synthesis of AI applications in anesthesiology and ICM. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications from January 2019 to December 2025 using the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “large language models,” “ChatGPT,” “anesthesiology,” “anesthesia,” “perioperative,” “intensive care,” and “critical care.” Studies with direct or potential clinical relevance to perioperative or intensive care practice were considered, and the selected literature was synthesized descriptively. Results: Forty-seven publications were included, encompassing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, narrative and scoping reviews, retrospective and prospective studies, randomized trials, and model development, validation, and evaluation studies. In anesthesiology, AI applications included preoperative risk stratification, difficult airway assessment, hemodynamic monitoring, closed-loop anesthesia, ultrasound-assisted procedures, postoperative outcome prediction, and perioperative communication. In ICM, major applications involved mortality and sepsis risk assessment, respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation management, intelligent alarm systems, delirium detection, sedation monitoring, and large language model (LLM)-assisted documentation. Although several approaches demonstrated promising predictive or supportive capabilities, prospective and randomized evidence remained limited. External validation, real-world clinical evaluation, data quality, model transparency, privacy, accountability, and regulatory uncertainty were recurring challenges. Conclusion: AI technologies have substantial potential to support clinical decision-making, situational awareness, individualized care, and workflow efficiency in anesthesiology and ICM. However, most applications remain in early stages of clinical translation. Current evidence supports their use as complementary, clinician-supervised tools rather than autonomous decision-makers. Robust prospective validation, standardized evaluation, ethical governance, and alignment with clinical needs are essential for safe and meaningful integration into routine practice.

documents.abstract: Power cables are the core power transmission carriers for modern urban power supply, and their safe and reliable operation is crucial to the stability of urban power grids. Traditional cable operation and maintenance (O&M) mainly relies on manual experience, suffers from prominent data silos, and struggles to meet the demands of complex power grids and high-reliability power supply. Data-driven artificial intelligence has been increasingly applied in cable O&M, serving as a complement to conventional operation frameworks. We focus on the O&M process oriented towards fault handling. Firstly, attention is paid to the core physical quantities for cable condition monitoring and the current application status of Internet of Things (IoT) sensing technology. Subsequently, the limitations of traditional fault diagnosis methods are systematically analyzed. Furthermore, we highlight the research progress of deep learning models such as attention mechanisms and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in cable fault diagnosis. Digital twin (DT) technology is also addressed, and its synergistic effect with AI technology in the intelligent O&M framework is systematically analyzed. Finally, we summarize the challenges faced in current technology implementation and look forward to future development directions.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed modern business environments by enhancing operational efficiency, supporting data-driven decision-making, and enabling the development of innovative business models. However, the widespread adoption of AI also introduces governance-related challenges, including issues of transparency, accountability, ethics, privacy, and regulatory compliance, making AI governance an increasingly important area of concern. This study aims to systematically review the existing literature on AI-driven business innovation and AI governance to identify current research trends, major themes, opportunities, and challenges in the field. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology was employed by collecting and analyzing relevant scholarly articles from major academic databases based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results reveal that AI contributes substantially to business innovation through process automation, predictive analytics, enhanced customer engagement, and strategic decision-making, while effective AI governance frameworks facilitate responsible AI adoption, strengthen stakeholder trust, and support sustainable digital transformation. The review further highlights that organizations achieving a balance between technological innovation and governance practices are better positioned to maximize the benefits of AI while mitigating potential risks. In conclusion, AI-driven business innovation and AI governance are mutually reinforcing factors that play a critical role in promoting sustainable business growth and long-term organizational competitiveness in the digital era.

documents.abstract: Abstract Climate change is creating serious problems for agriculture by increasing drought, soil salinity, and extreme temperatures. These stresses affect plant growth, development, crop yield, and global food security. Traditional methods used to study plant responses to stress are often time-consuming, labour-intensive, and difficult to use for large numbers of plants. Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important tool for studying and predicting plant responses to changing environmental conditions. AI can analyse large amounts of data collected through plant phenotyping, remote sensing, environmental sensors, and molecular studies. This review focuses on recent AI approaches used to predict plant responses to drought, salinity, and temperature stress from 2016 to 2026. Machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, thermal imaging, and hyperspectral imaging can help in early detection and prediction of plant stress. Recent developments are moving beyond simple stress identification towards predicting crop performance and stress tolerance. The combination of AI with high-throughput phenotyping and multi-omics can help identify stress-tolerant crop varieties and support climate-resilient breeding. However, challenges related to data quality, limited field validation, unclear model predictions, and poor performance across different environments still remain. Future research should develop reliable and explainable AI models for sustainable agriculture and improved crop production under climate change.

Abstract Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into intensive care unit (ICU) ventilator management has attracted growing research interest, with studies exploring applications ranging from surveillance and decision support toward more autonomous ventilatory adjustment. Whether this represents a clinically validated transition from reactive to proactive ventilation management remains to be established through prospective evidence. This review maps the available literature on these developments in the context of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI), a heterogeneous syndrome including barotrauma, volutrauma, atelectrauma, and biotrauma. This review maps AI applications relevant to VILI detection and prevention, rather than studies that directly demonstrate VILI prevention. Methods This scoping review mapped and synthesized evidence on the use of AI-based systems for the early detection and prevention of VILI in critically ill adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and the Biblioteca Virtual en Salud (BVS) for literature published between 2010 and 2026. Results A total of 52 studies met full-text inclusion criteria. Most AI applications focused on automated detection of patient-ventilator asynchronies, prediction of complications related to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and optimization of lung-protective ventilation parameters through machine learning and reinforcement learning approaches. Although AI-based systems may support more individualized ventilatory management strategies, their clinical implementation remains limited by the lack of external validation, methodological heterogeneity, and scarce evidence in low- and middle-income settings. Conclusions The evidence identified is predominantly technical, retrospective and exploratory, and rests largely on surrogate physiological or classification endpoints. High diagnostic accuracy, or improvement in surrogate parameters, does not by itself constitute evidence that these systems prevent VILI or improve patient-centred outcomes. Current evidence therefore supports the promise of these applications and the prioritization of prospective research, but not their routine clinical implementation.

The scarcity of global water resources has made irrigation optimization a key challenge for sustainable agriculture. Rice cultivation, one of the most water-intensive cropping systems, offers significant opportunities for improving water-use efficiency through artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This systematic review evaluates the application of AI techniques for irrigation optimization in rice farming within the context of Agriculture 4.0, with the aim of identifying the principal AI approaches, application domains, research trends, and future directions. The review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines using publications retrieved from ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library published over the past five years. Fourteen studies meeting the predefined eligibility criteria were selected for qualitative synthesis and bibliometric analysis. The results indicate that machine learning and deep learning approaches, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Random Forest (RF) models, dominate the current literature. These methods are primarily applied to irrigation scheduling, crop water requirement prediction, soil moisture estimation, and yield forecasting. The analysis also reveals a strong geographical concentration of research in Asia, which accounts for 64.3% of the selected studies. Furthermore, data availability remains limited, with half of the datasets accessible only upon request and only 7.1% publicly available, highlighting an important barrier to reproducibility and broader adoption of AI-based irrigation solutions. Emerging research directions include the integration of remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, and intelligent decision support systems to enable adaptive, data-driven irrigation management. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of AI-enabled irrigation optimization in rice farming, identifies existing research gaps, and outlines future opportunities for developing sustainable intelligent irrigation systems.

Abstract Green chemistry seeks to prevent pollution at its source by reducing waste, energy demand, hazardous substances, and resource consumption. Artificial intelligence (AI), especially machine learning (ML), can strengthen this approach by learning from chemical and process data, predicting outcomes, screening large chemical spaces, and optimizing experiments. Recent literature identifies applications ranging from catalyst discovery and reaction optimization to CO₂ capture, sustainable polymers, waste management, water treatment, and process control. A 2026 review in Applied Intelligence highlights artificial neural networks, random forests, and Bayesian optimization as important approaches across these areas, while also emphasizing data quality, validation, energy use, and scalability as major concerns. (see References 1–6) This project reviews how AI can support the principles of green chemistry and proposes a practical research framework in which sustainability metrics are included directly in model objectives. The central idea is that an AI system should not merely maximize chemical yield; it should seek a balanced outcome involving yield, selectivity, waste, toxicity, energy, solvent impact, and resource efficiency. The report concludes that AI can become an enabling technology for greener chemistry when models are transparent, experimentally validated, and evaluated against environmental as well as technical performance.

Acute Care Surgery (ACS) emerged not as a single innovation, but as the progressive integration of operative discipline, intensive care, trauma systems, biologically informed resuscitation, and regionalized care infrastructure into a layered, complex, adaptive system. Artificial intelligence (AI) now represents the next major technological layer being introduced into this mature sociotechnical environment. This narrative review examines ACS from a systems perspective and argues that the success or failure of AI integration requires both algorithmic performance and how effectively these technologies couple with existing workflows, operational structures, feedback mechanisms, and clinical decision-making processes. Historical developments in ACS - including intensive care evolution, trauma system regionalization, damage control philosophy, and prior failures of reductionist biologic interventions - provide important lessons for understanding the opportunities and risks of AI deployment in high-acuity surgical care. Current AI applications in ACS include augmented diagnostics, continuous physiologic surveillance, predictive analytics, operative video analysis, workflow optimization, and educational assessment. However, important issues remain, including alert fatigue, automation bias, implementation failure, inequitable model generalizability, and the risks of introducing reductionist computational paradigms into complex adaptive systems. A systems-oriented framework emphasizes that AI tools must be evaluated not as isolated products, but as components of broader clinical, organizational, and educational ecosystems. ACS, with its longstanding experience integrating layered technologies and coordinating multidisciplinary care under conditions of uncertainty, may represent one of the most informative environments in which to study responsible AI implementation in surgery.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transitioning from a supportive tool to a core component of clinical decision-making in dentistry. This review synthesizes advances in deep learning and machine learning for oral disease diagnosis, orthodontic treatment prediction, pediatric oral health management, adolescent psychological-oral health interactions, and precision care for special-needs populations, drawing on evidence published predominantly between 2024 and 2026. A systematic search across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus identified 30 studies for narrative synthesis. Several AI models reported higher diagnostic or predictive performance than selected conventional comparators in detecting periodontal bone loss, temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis, and oral squamous cell carcinoma, with accuracy frequently exceeding 90%. In orthodontics, AI-driven prediction reduces tooth movement error rates substantially. However, most studies rely on single-center retrospective data lacking prospective multicenter validation. Future priorities include multimodal data fusion, federated learning, and standardized validation frameworks to facilitate clinical translation.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become part of contemporary visual communication and is changing the way graphic designers generate, develop, refine, and present ideas. Tools based on generative AI can produce images, illustrations, layouts, typography suggestions, visual variations, and creative concepts within seconds. For graphic designers, this development offers significant opportunities for experimentation and efficiency, but it also raises important questions about creativity, originality, authorship, professional identity, and the future of design education. This paper explores the relationship between artificial intelligence and graphic design from the perspective of creative practice. The paper argues that AI does not eliminate the need for human creativity; instead, it changes where creative effort takes place. Designers increasingly need to formulate problems, evaluate generated possibilities, make cultural and aesthetic judgments, refine outputs, and give visual communication a meaningful human direction. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI may lead to design fixation, visual similarity, weakened foundational skills, and uncertainty regarding authorship. The paper concludes that the most productive future for graphic design lies in responsible human–AI collaboration, supported by strong foundations in design principles, visual thinking, ethics, and critical judgment.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the design industry by introducing data-driven, generative, predictive, and automated approaches to creative and technical processes. Interior design, traditionally dependent on human creativity, spatial understanding, material knowledge, and client preferences, is increasingly influenced by AI-powered tools capable of generating design concepts, visualizations, layouts, material combinations, lighting solutions, and personalized spatial recommendations. Recent developments in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal systems have expanded the possibilities for designers to explore a larger number of alternatives in less time. This research paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future perspectives associated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence into interior design. The study adopts a qualitative systematic literature review approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-assisted architectural and built-environment design. The review indicates that AI can support concept generation, space planning, 3D visualization, material selection, sustainability analysis, personalization, and client communication. However, issues related to creativity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, data privacy, professional responsibility, design authenticity, technical skills, and overdependence on automated systems remain significant challenges. Recent systematic reviews show that AI research in design is strongly concentrated in early conceptual and schematic stages, while later stages requiring detailed technical, contextual, and professional judgment remain comparatively underexplored. The paper argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for interior designers but as an augmentation technology that can strengthen human creativity, decision-making, and productivity. A human-centred AI framework combining technological capability with professional expertise, ethical safeguards, cultural sensitivity, and user participation is proposed. The study concludes that the future of interior design will increasingly depend on effective human–AI collaboration rather than complete automation.
